concept: MongoDB Advanced Explain: Aggregation, Sharded Plans, Loose Index Scans and the 8.3 Cost-Based Ranker
summary: Advanced explain output covers spill statistics for blocking aggregation stages (usedDisk, spilledBytes and the per-stage memory limit), sharded plans (SHARD_MERGE, splitPipeline with shardsPart and mergerPart, mergeType), the $sort+$group $first loose index scan that explain reports as DISTINCT_SCAN, and the 8.3 cost-based ranker with its costEstimate and cardinalityEstimate fields. Compiled from MongoDB manual and JIRA pages plus the run's verified claims.

facts.text: Classic multi-planner winner is the plan that produces the most results during the trial while doing the least work; the winning multi-planner score is reported in explain executionStats-era fields, distinct from CBR costEstimate.

Planning time (optimizationTimeMillis) excludes time spent optimizing inner $lookup queries. Since 8.0 rejectedPlans contain only the find portion; earlier versions could include aggregation stages such as $group.

Starting in MongoDB 9.0, when you run `explain` in a mimumum of [executionStats](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/db.collection.explain.md#std-label-explain-method-executionStats) verbosity mode, aggregation stages that use the classic query execution engine output a `expressionEvaluationPeakMemoryBytes` field. This field contains the peak memory usage, in bytes, from expression evaluation during stage execution.

The explain field mergeType reports where the merger part runs; the documented examples show mongos and anyShard. Search summaries of the docs also list specificShard (with a mergeShard field naming the shard) and router, but the page text for those was not directly verified.

If you run [`explain`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/explain.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.explain) on a `$setWindowsFields` operation, the output contains a `peakTrackedMemBytes` field that contains the maximum number of bytes of tracked memory in use. For more information, see [`explain.executionStats.peakTrackedMemBytes`.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/explain-results.md#mongodb-data-explain.executionStats.peakTrackedMemBytes)

When you downgrade the FCV from `9.0` to an earlier version, a migration updates the stored query settings. The migration removes every knob whose minimum FCV exceeds the target version and deletes any settings entry that still contains only default values. Re-upgrading to `9.0` does not restore the removed knobs. You must re-apply them with `setQuerySettings`.

The second case occurs when the merge part of the split pipeline contains a stage which may write temporary data to disk, such as $group, and the client has specified allowDiskUse:true. In this case, assuming that there are no other stages in the merge pipeline which require the primary shard, the merge runs on a randomly-selected shard in the set of shards targeted by the aggregation.
The random-shard merge exists so the merger part has more disk space available for spilling blocking stages when allowDiskUse is true; with allowDiskUse false, streaming-only mergers stay on mongos.

The first case occurs when the merge part of the split pipeline contains a stage which *must* run on a specific shard. For instance, if `$lookup` requires access to an unsharded collection in the same database as the sharded collection on which the aggregation is running, the merge runs on the shard that hosts the unsharded collection.
Contains partial execution information captured during the plan selection phase for both the winning and rejected plans. The field is present only if explain runs in allPlansExecution verbosity mode.
Object that contains two fields: true and false. Each field counts the number of matching queries where the value of usedDisk is true or false, respectively.
When splitting the aggregation pipeline into two parts, the pipeline is split to ensure that the shards perform as many stages as possible with consideration for optimization.
Contains metrics related to CBR when it is used during query planning. CBR evaluates multiple query plans and selects the most efficient plan based on estimated costs.
Contains metrics related to the number of documents sampled during cost-based ranking for queries with the given key.
Contains counts for each cardinality estimation method used during cost-based ranking. Each field represents the number of times a particular estimation method was used.

mergeType shows where the stage of the merge happens ("anyShard", "specificShard", or "router"). When mergeType is specificShard, the aggregate output includes a mergeShard property that contains the shard ID of the merging shard.
If the query optimizer uses the cost-based ranker, the output contains several additional fields.

CVE-2026-4358 (published 2026-03-17): a crafted $lookup aggregation by an authenticated user with write privileges can trigger a double-free or use-after-free in the SBE engine when an in-memory hash table is spilled to disk. CVSS v4 6.1 medium, v3 7.5.

Starting in MongoDB 8.3, multi-planning with a CBR backup is the default plan selection mechanism for eligible queries. For a short trial period, the multi-planner attempts to find a plan capable of returning a result set within this short timeframe. If the attempt is unsuccessful, MongoDB applies a set of rules to determine whether the multi-planner should continue or if CBR should evaluate each node in the plan to determine the optimal plan.

Explain output for CBR plans adds costEstimate, cardinalityEstimate, numKeysEstimate, numDocsEstimate and estimatesMetadata.ceSource per stage, marked new in 8.3.3. ceSource values: sampling, heuristics (only when sampling fails), mixed, metadata, code. A large gap between numKeysEstimate and costEstimate can indicate a problem with the winning plan.

Percona lists reduced multi-planning cost among 8.3 performance improvements and says the new serverStatus counters and explain output show when CBR was used and how often it won; it gives no CBR-specific benchmark.

Merge location rules: if the pipeline starts with an exact $match on the shard key and has no $out or $lookup, the whole pipeline runs on the one matching shard (no split); otherwise results merge on mongos, except $out/$lookup cases and a randomly selected shard when a sort or group stage runs with allowDiskUse enabled.

When explain is run in either executionStats or allPlansExecution verbosity mode, certain aggregation stages that may spill to disk have additional output. These stages include $sort, $group, $setWindowFields, $bucketAuto, $graphLookup, and $lookup (when using the slot-based execution engine). Starting in MongoDB 8.1, this also includes $text queries that use the TextOr execution stage.

Starting in MongoDB 9.0 a per-operation memory limit (internalQueryMaxMemoryUsageBytesPerOperation, default max of 1 GB or 20% of server memory) covers combined tracked memory of blocking stages and expressions. It does not change per-stage spilling. Overruns return QueryExceededMemoryLimitNoDiskUseAllowed (292, when allowDiskUse is false) or ExceededMemoryLimit (146).

Since MongoDB 6.0 the allowDiskUseByDefault parameter decides whether stages needing more than 100 MB of memory write temporary files (true) or raise an error (false). Per-command {allowDiskUse: true|false} overrides it.

$push and $addToSet inside $group cannot spill: each hits a separate 100 MB cap and fails with 'used too much memory and cannot spill to disk. Memory limit: 104857600 bytes' even with allowDiskUse: true. Fix by restructuring (filter or limit first, two-step group, $topN), not by flag.
Profiler and diagnostic log lines carry a usedDisk indicator when any stage wrote temporary files, so spills show up in slow-query logs without re-running explain.

Mitigations for memory pressure: use an index-backed sort, put $limit after $sort, and filter with $match early. On sharded clusters, allowDiskUse on a sorting or grouping stage may move the merge to a randomly selected shard.

Starting in MongoDB 8.3, the query engine limits the `TextOr` stage memory usage to 100 megabytes. The `TextOr` stage processes [`$text`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/text.md#mongodb-query-op.-text) queries that read text score metadata. For example, `TextOr` processes queries that sort results by text score. If the `TextOr` stage exceeds this limit:
Starting in MongoDB 9.0, MongoDB limits the total amount of memory that a single query operation can use. The limit applies to the combined memory of all memory-tracked stages of the operation.

To check if MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort, append cursor.explain() to the query and check the explain results. If the query plan contains a SORT stage, then MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort operation subject to the 100 megabyte memory limit.

planCacheShapeHash (added 8.0, duplicate of deprecated queryHash) depends only on query shape; planCacheKey depends on shape plus available indexes, so adding or dropping an index changes the key but not the shape hash.

Third-party guidance calls CBR the primary plan-regression risk in an 8.0 to 8.3 upgrade (claimed 5-50x slowdowns on some shapes) and recommends capturing plan shapes before upgrade and diffing after. This is an unquantified vendor-blog opinion, not measured evidence; no independent benchmark of CBR plan quality was found.

Starting in MongoDB 9.0, MongoDB tracks the memory that [`$nearSphere`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/query/nearsphere.md#mongodb-query-op.-nearSphere) uses to buffer results and to remove duplicate records. If the query exceeds the 100 megabyte memory limit for the stage, MongoDB ends the query and returns an error.
Statistics for the $queryStats stage are tracked in a virtual collection that is stored in-memory. The memory limit for the virtual collection is 1% of the system's total memory.

When a query shape has query knobs set through setQuerySettings or setParameter, slow query log entries include a queryKnobs document. The document shows the effective value of each knob and where the value comes from, with the same shape as the explain output. For details, see Query Knobs.

Aggregation pipelines which call `$bottom` are subject to the [100 MB limit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-agg-memory-restrictions). If this limit is exceeded for an individual group, the aggregation fails with an error.

To change the per-operation limit, set the [`internalQueryMaxMemoryUsageBytesPerOperation`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.internalQueryMaxMemoryUsageBytesPerOperation) parameter at startup, at runtime, or with query settings.

For memory-intensive expressions that the per-operation limit does not cover, MongoDB applies a limit on the maximum memory that a subset of expressions can use. The default of this limit is 100 megabytes. To change this limit, set the [`internalQueryMaxSingleExpressionMemoryUsageBytes`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.internalQueryMaxSingleExpressionMemoryUsageBytes) parameter at startup or at runtime.

To learn more, see [$sort and $limit Memory Optimization.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/sort.md#std-label-sort-limit-sequence)

Some stages can't output any documents until they have processed all incoming documents. These pipeline stages must keep their stage output in RAM until all incoming documents are processed. As a result, these pipeline stages may require more space than the 100 MB limit.

If the [`$group`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/group.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-group) stage exceeds 100 megabytes of RAM, MongoDB writes data to temporary files. However, if the [allowDiskUse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/aggregate.md#std-label-aggregate-cmd-allowDiskUse) option is set to `false`, `$group` returns an error. For more information, refer to [aggregation pipeline limits.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-agg-pipeline-limits)

If MongoDB cannot obtain the sort order with an index scan, then MongoDB uses a top-k sort algorithm. This algorithm buffers the first `k` results (or last, depending on the sort order) seen so far by the underlying index or collection access. If the memory footprint of these `k` results exceeds 100 megabytes, MongoDB automatically writes temporary files to disk unless the query specifies [`cursor.allowDiskUse()`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/method/cursor.allowdiskuse.md#mongodb-method-cursor.allowDiskUse) with a value of `false` (in which case, the query fails).

createIndexes supports building one or more indexes on a collection. createIndexes uses a combination of memory and temporary files on disk to build indexes. In self-hosted MongoDB deployments, the default value of the maxIndexBuildMemoryUsageMegabytes parameter is 200 megabytes per createIndexes command. createIndexes shares the memory limit equally among all the indexes it builds. For example, if you build 10 indexes with one createIndexes command, MongoDB allocates each index 20 megabytes for the index build process. When you reach the memory limit, MongoDB creates temporary files in the _t

In self-hosted MongoDB deployments, you can change the memory limit for index builds by setting the maxIndexBuildMemoryUsageMegabytes parameter. Increasing this parameter is only necessary in rare cases. Such cases include running many simultaneous index builds with a single createIndexes command or indexing a data set larger than 500GB. You can also set maxNumActiveUserIndexBuilds to adjust how many index builds can run concurrently.

If the [`$graphLookup`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/graphlookup.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-graphLookup) stage exceeds 100 megabytes of memory and the `allowDiskUse` option is set to `false`, [`$graphLookup`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/operator/aggregation/graphlookup.md#mongodb-pipeline-pipe.-graphLookup) returns an error.

Only queries that match a large number of documents reach the limit. To reduce the memory that the query requires, specify `maxDistance` to restrict the search area. This memory counts toward the per-operation memory limit. To learn more, see [Per-Operation Memory Limit.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-operation-memory-limit)
- If `allowDiskUse` is `false`, the query fails with an exceeded memory limit error.
In earlier versions, the `TextOr` stage had no memory limit and consumed RAM without restrictions, risking out-of-memory (OOM) errors.

- If [`allowDiskUseByDefault`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/parameters.md#mongodb-parameter-param.allowDiskUseByDefault) is set to `false`, pipeline stages that require more than 100 megabytes of memory to execute raise an error by default. You can enable writing temporary files to disk for specific `find` or `aggregate` using the `{ allowDiskUse: true }` option.

In addition to the per-stage limit, a single operation can use no more memory than the [per-operation memory limit.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-operation-memory-limit)

The per-operation limit is separate from the 100 megabyte per-stage memory limit and doesn't change how stages spill to disk. To learn about the per-stage limit, see [Memory Restrictions.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-agg-memory-restrictions)

This parameter sets the [per-operation memory limit](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-operation-memory-limit). To learn which stages and expressions MongoDB tracks and what happens when an operation exceeds the limit, see [Per-Operation Memory Limit.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-operation-memory-limit)

MongoDB applies this limit when the per-operation memory limit does not apply to the operation. To learn about the per-operation memory limit, see [Per-Operation Memory Limit.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-operation-memory-limit)

As each stage in a `$facet` executes, the resulting document is limited to 100 megabytes. Note the [allowDiskUse](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/aggregate.md#std-label-aggregate-cmd-allowDiskUse) flag doesn't affect the 100 megabyte size limit, since `$facet` can't spill to disk.
The view's underlying aggregation pipeline is subject to the 100 megabyte memory limit for blocking sort and blocking group operations.

Use allowDiskUse() to either allow or prohibit writing temporary files on disk when a pipeline stage exceeds the 100 megabyte limit. Starting in MongoDB 6.0, operations that require greater than 100 megabytes of memory automatically write data to temporary files by default.

Since reading.timestamp is not included in an index, MongoDB must perform an in-memory sort operation to return results in the requested sort order. By specifying cursor.allowDiskUse(false), MongoDB cannot process the sort operation if it requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory. If the operation requires more than 100 megabytes of system memory, MongoDB would return an error.

The optimization still applies when `allowDiskUse` is `true` and the `n` items exceed the [aggregation memory limit.](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/aggregation-pipeline-limits.md#std-label-agg-memory-restrictions)

Current configured value of the maximum amount of memory in bytes that all memory-tracked stages of a single query operation may collectively use. Use this metric to correlate failures with the configured memory limit.
Number of times since startup that a query operation failed because it exceeded memory-tracking limits. Use this metric to determine whether the memory limit is too low for your workload.
Largest amount of memory in bytes tracked for a single operation since startup. Use this metric to determine an appropriate per-operation memory limit for your workload.

An [initial sync](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-sync.md#std-label-replica-set-sync) populates only one collection at a time and has no risk of exceeding the memory limit. However, it is possible for a user to start index builds on multiple collections in multiple databases simultaneously.

To view the [`memory limit`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/hostinfo.md#mongodb-data-hostInfo.system.memLimitMB), the value that WiredTiger utilizes as the maximum amount of RAM available use the [`hostInfo`](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/command/hostinfo.md#mongodb-dbcommand-dbcmd.hostInfo) command.

For any given query, the MongoDB query planner chooses and caches an efficient query plan given the available indexes. The planner can use either the classic multi-planner or the cost-based ranker (CBR) to select a plan.

If the attempt is unsuccessful, MongoDB applies a set of rules to decide whether the multi-planner should continue or if CBR should evaluate the plans to determine the optimal solution. CBR evaluates each node in a plan based on a cost function and its cardinality estimations. MongoDB selects the plan with the lowest overall cost as the winning plan. Currently, MongoDB only invokes the CBR for a small amount of queries.
